content.summary: Welcome to Unit 1! In this reading module, you will explore texts about remarkable people, discover how to describe personality traits, and master the differences between the present perfect and past simple tenses. You will also learn how to use helper words like just, already, and yet.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present Perfect with just, already, and yet compared with Past Simple
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Personality adjectives such as brave, charming, creative, talented, laid-back, positive, active, and cheerful
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming paragraphs for general topics and scanning specific sentences for key details and time markers

rules: Present Perfect + just: Use 'just' for actions completed very recently. Example: I have just finished my homework.
Present Perfect + already: Use 'already' for actions completed sooner than expected. Example: She has already come back from Papua New Guinea.
Present Perfect + yet: Use 'yet' in questions and negative sentences for things we expect to happen. Example: They haven't made any recordings yet.
Past Simple for specific times: Use past simple when the exact time in the past is mentioned. Example: She wrote her first book when she was just five.
Present Perfect for life experiences: Use present perfect when the exact time is not important. Example: He has visited Greece more than 20 times.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often mix up the past simple and the present perfect when talking about recent actions with time words.
commonTrap.wrong: I have visited my grandparents yesterday.
commonTrap.correct: I visited my grandparents yesterday. (Use past simple for specific past time words like yesterday).

paragraphs: Meet Maya, a sixteen-year-old artist from London. Maya is incredibly creative and has already painted over fifty portraits of local community heroes. Last year, she won a national art prize for her inspiring work. Even though she is busy with school, she remains relaxed and cheerful every single day.

Then there is Leo, a brave young explorer who has just returned from an expedition in the Amazon rainforest. Leo is active, curious, and deeply passionate about wildlife protection. He has visited five different countries this year alone, talking to students about environmental care. He has not written his book about the journey yet, but everyone is excited to read it when it comes out.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize proper names, nationalities, and days of the week.
mechanicsRules.badExample: sarah lives in london and speaks spanish.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Sarah lives in London and speaks Spanish.
mechanicsRules.why: Proper nouns and adjectives of nationality require capital letters in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place 'already' and 'just' between auxiliary verbs and past participles.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Mark has finished already his difficult project.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Mark has already finished his difficult project.
mechanicsRules.why: Adverbs of time like already and just sit before the main verb in present perfect sentences.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use commas after introductory time clauses or transition phrases.
mechanicsRules.badExample: When she was young she loved reading biography books.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: When she was young, she loved reading biography books.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates a dependent introductory clause from the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following affirmative sentence into a complete negative sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Luke enjoys playing video games after dinner.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'does not enjoy' or 'doesn't enjoy'.
targetAnswers: Luke doesn't enjoy playing video games after dinner.
Luke does not enjoy playing video games after dinner.
practicumQuestions.explanation: With third-person singular subjects like Luke, use 'does not' or 'doesn't' followed by the base verb 'enjoy'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'has just' to show a very recent action:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Emma finished her English project a moment ago.
practicumQuestions.hint: Insert 'has just' before the past participle of 'finish'.
targetAnswers: Emma has just finished her English project.
Emma has just finished her English project
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present perfect with 'just' uses 'has/have + just + past participle' to describe actions completed moments ago.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with the correct conjunction (although, because, or so):
practicumQuestions.promptText: Mark is very shy, ________ he speaks confidently when giving presentations.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use a conjunction that shows contrast between being shy and speaking confidently.
targetAnswers: although

practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Although' is used to introduce a contrasting idea or unexpected contrast.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence with correct capitalization and punctuation:
practicumQuestions.promptText: anna lives in paris and studies French on mondays.
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize proper names, cities, languages, and days of the week.
targetAnswers: Anna lives in Paris and studies French on Mondays.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Anna, Paris, French, and Mondays are proper nouns or proper adjectives and must always be capitalized in English.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence into the negative present perfect using 'yet':
practicumQuestions.promptText: They did not finish the report.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'haven't finished' and place 'yet' at the end of the sentence.
targetAnswers: They haven't finished the report yet.
They have not finished the report yet.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In negative present perfect sentences, 'yet' is placed at the very end to indicate something has not happened up to now.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the past simple sentence into the present perfect using 'already':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Sarah bought her ticket to London this morning.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'has already bought'.
targetAnswers: Sarah has already bought her ticket to London.
Sarah has already bought her ticket to London
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'has already' with the past participle ('bought') to indicate an action completed sooner than expected.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose the correct connector to show cause and effect:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Liam studied hard for the test, ________ he got an excellent grade.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the conjunction that means 'therefore' or 'as a result'.
targetAnswers: so
So
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'So' connects a cause (studying hard) with its direct result (getting an excellent grade).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the grammar error regarding auxiliary verbs in the sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: she have already visited her grandparents in sydney.
practicumQuestions.hint: Third-person singular pronouns (she) use 'has', not 'have'.
targetAnswers: She has already visited her grandparents in Sydney.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The subject 'she' requires the auxiliary verb 'has', and 'Sydney' requires a capital letter.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Unscramble and write the words into a correct present continuous sentence describing a current action:
practicumQuestions.promptText: [ is / writing / she / book / an / inspiring / now ]
practicumQuestions.hint: Subject + is + verb-ing + complement.
targetAnswers: She is writing an inspiring book now.
She is writing an inspiring book right now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present continuous tense is formed with 'is' and the '-ing' form of the verb to describe actions happening right now.

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practice talking about amazing people, describing personalities using adjectives, and using present tenses correctly. Clear pronunciation and correct sentence stress make your spoken English sound natural and easy to understand.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to syllable stress in personality adjectives like creative and talented. When speaking, link your words smoothly and use appropriate intonation to show your feelings.

pillars.name: Syllable Stress
pillars.target: Accurate stress placement in multi-syllable adjectives
pillars.explanation: English words have stressed syllables that are louder and longer. Getting stress right helps listeners understand your description of people.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.target: Smooth linking between words in present tense sentences
pillars.explanation: Native speakers link final consonant sounds to initial vowel sounds, making speech flow naturally without awkward pauses.

pillars.name: Sentence Intonation
pillars.target: Proper use of rising and falling pitch for statements and questions
pillars.explanation: Use falling intonation for statements and wh-questions, and rising intonation for yes-no questions or showing uncertainty.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the main stress remains strong on the adjective while adverbs modify the degree.
Stress falls on the second syllable of creative.
The primary stress is on the first syllable of talented.
Compound adjectives like laid-back keep primary stress on the first element.
